summary: A beit din (literally 'house of judgment') is a rabbinical court, the Jewish judicial institution that adjudicates matters of halakha. The tradition roots the institution in the biblical command to appoint judges 'in all your gates', and the rabbinic sources set out its structure: a court of three judges for ordinary cases, larger courts for graver matters, and, in the Second Temple period, the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one as the supreme court. A beit din hears such matters as conversions, divorces (issuing the get), and monetary and communal disputes, and it remains a functioning institution in Jewish communal life.
description:
A beit din (Hebrew for 'house of judgment', plural batei din) is a court of Jewish law, the judicial institution through which the community adjudicates matters of halakha. The tradition, described here on its own terms, roots the institution in the Torah's command at Deuteronomy 16:18, 'You shall appoint magistrates and officials (shoftim ve-shotrim) for your tribes, in all your gates (bekhol she'arekha) ... and they shall govern the people with due justice', taken as the mandate to establish courts throughout the community.

The rabbinic sources set out the court's structure. The Mishnah, in the opening chapter of tractate Sanhedrin, lays out a graded system: ordinary cases of monetary law, and cases of robbery and personal injury, are judged by a court of three (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:1); graver matters require larger courts; and at the summit stand two rabbinic courts of the Second Temple period, 'the Great Sanhedrin was of seventy-one judges, and a lesser Sanhedrin was of twenty-three' (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6), the number seventy-one derived from the seventy elders gathered with Moses (Numbers 11:16) together with Moses at their head. The Great Sanhedrin functioned as the supreme court and central legislative-judicial body of the tradition in that period.

Beyond adjudicating disputes, the beit din carries out functions that require a formal court: it oversees conversion to Judaism (giyyur), it is required for the writing and delivery of a bill of divorce (the get), and it rules on questions of personal status and of monetary and communal law. In contemporary Jewish life the beit din remains a working institution: communities maintain courts, often of three, that handle conversions, divorces, dietary and ritual certification, and civil disputes brought for adjudication or arbitration under Jewish law. This entry describes the beit din on the tradition's own terms as the community's legal-judicial institution and reports its structure and authority as the tradition's account, without adjudicating the halakhic questions it exists to decide.
editorial_notes:
This entry treats the beit din as a sociological and institutional concept: the religious community's legal-judicial institution, the court through which halakha is adjudicated and applied. It is described on Judaism's own terms (neutrality #1, #4, #6), and its structure and authority are recorded as the tradition's account rather than adjudicated.

Sourcing triangulates the three lenses per neutrality #8. (b) The primary corpus was read openly and line-by-line on Sefaria: Deuteronomy 16:18, the command to appoint 'judges and officers ... in all your gates' (shoftim ve-shotrim ... bekhol she'arekha), which carries the biblical root of the institution, and Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:1-1:6, which carries the structure (three judges for ordinary cases; the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one and the lesser of twenty-three). These load-bearing passages are rated high. relations.note: The beit din is the institution that adjudicates and applies halakha; the court exists to decide questions of Jewish law and to render binding rulings within the community. The law and the court that administers it are the linked halves of the rabbinic legal system.

In the classical account, ordination (semikhah) qualified its holders to sit on a beit din and to adjudicate specified categories of law; the court and the ordination that empowered its judges are the linked institutions of rabbinic legal authority. semikhah exists in the dataset.

The Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one judges (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6) was, in the Second Temple period, the supreme beit din and central judicial-legislative body of the tradition; the ordinary beit din of three sits at the base of the graded system the Sanhedrin crowned.

Both address the religious community's judicial institution, the seat that adjudicates the community's law. The beit din is a collegial court, classically of three (or, at its summit, the Sanhedrin), that decides matters of halakha; in Islam the qadi is the judge who adjudicates cases according to the sharia, sitting in the sharia courts. The link marks a shared question about the community's judicial institution and an explicit difference in the answer, a collegial rabbinical court versus the office of the single judge of the sharia court, and ranks neither.

Both address the religious community's law and the judicial institution that administers it. The beit din adjudicates halakha through a court of Jewish law; canon law is the body of ecclesiastical law of the Christian churches, administered in its own church courts and tribunals. The link marks a shared question about the community's judicial-legal institution and an explicit difference in the answer, a rabbinical court applying halakha versus church tribunals applying canon law, and ranks neither. canon-law exists in the dataset.

historical_period.note: The tradition roots the institution in the Torah's command to appoint judges (Deuteronomy 16:18), for which a conventional and approximate date is given; the graded court system and the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one belong to the Second Temple and early rabbinic periods (the Mishnah's account redacted around 200 CE), and the beit din remains a living institution in Jewish communal life, so no end date is asserted. Dates are conventional and mark a long development rather than a single origin.
